new_statements.quote: All four languages make use of tones, or “musical intonations,” but in no case do these appear to be semantic. The primary accent in a word, or sometimes in a cluster of words, is frequently accorded the highest pitch, the secondary accent medium pitch, and unaccented syllables the lowest pitch. [...] Nevertheless, the position of an accent in all these languages may be semantically critical: e.g. (in Kafe) ‘ka:nina, “banana”; ka:'ni:na, “maggot,” or “grub” [...]. Stress is indicated in this paper only when it does not fall on the first syllable.
new_statements.citation: Berndt, Catherine H. 1954. Translation problems in three New Guinea Highland languages. Oceania 24(4): 289-317.
new_statements.locator: p. 293, section 'Phonetics' (issue p. 55; p. 5 of the extracted article PDF)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. Berndt 1954 pp.289-290 (mirror PDF text): Jate's 'main sub-groups are the Ke'zjagana or Keijagana Jate about Taramu' (so identity is right), but she adds 'My husband has concentrated on Jate.. whereas my information concerning it is fragmentary. This paper, then, will deal with the three languages with which I am personally familiar, and will refer to Jate only incidentally.' The p.293 prosody paragraph ('All four languages..', Kafe minimal pair) is therefore a blanket claim not grounded in her own Jate/Keyagana data. | checker: Opened the saved whole-issue scanned (lines 4413-4425) and : the passage is on p. 293 under 'Phonetics' exactly as A quotes…
new_statements.relation_note: Tone present but non-phonemic per author; contrastive accent position possible; default-initial stress implied by marking convention.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Kafe, Uturupa, Fo:re and Jate (incl. Ke'jagana = Keyagana): pitch ('tones') is present but judged non-contrastive, tracking accent (primary accent = highest pitch, secondary = mid, unaccented = low); word accent exists and its position can distinguish words (Kafe minimal pair given); the author's transcription convention marks stress only when it is NOT on the first syllable, i.e. initial stress is treated as the default/commonest position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: A 'secondary accent' with medium pitch is mentioned; no placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent 'rather more important in Fo:re than in the other languages, especially perhaps in certain verb forms'; tones 'often dispensed with'; accent domain 'a word, or sometimes.. a cluster of words'.
new_statements.identity_note: The paper treats Kafe (Kamano), Uturupa (Usarufa) and Fo:re in detail and 'Jate' incidentally; Berndt defines Jate's main sub-groups as 'the Ke'jagana or Keijagana Jate about Taramu; the Kemiju and Henagaru Jate; and the Friganu Jate' and used Ke'jagana/Kemiju Jate as a working medium (fieldwork 1951-53, Taramu/Okapa area). Ke'jagana/Keijagana Jate = Keyagana (keya1238); Glottolog codes this article to Keyagana. The prosody sentences are asserted for 'all four languages' (Kafe, Uturupa, Fo:re, Jate); the worked example is Kafe (kama1370), and the author states her Jate knowledge is 'fragmentary'. | group-level statement: Ford treats Kamano, Yate and Yagaria as one dialect network 'K-Y' and lists 'Yate, Ke'yagana, Kanite' as its group (c) dialect names (p. 193); the idiolects actually analysed are Huva, Yate (Nupagimi village), Move, Kami and Kafe, none from a Keyagana village, so the statement applies to Keyagana only as a named member of K-Y [name in source: Ke'yagana (listed with Yate and Kanite as dialect names of Kamano-Yagaria, 'K-Y'); pages 191-202 (Ke'yagana named p. 193; tone statement p. 195; tone systems of the analysed dialects pp. 196-201)]

new_statements.quote: The dialect names used in the literature for K-Y are: a. Kamano, Kafe b. Huva, Hila, Kamate, Filigano, Move, Kami, Oligutili, Kotomi, Dagenava c. Yate, Ke'yagana, Kanite [p. 193] ... K-Y is a lexical tone language on the following bases: a. as in every language, each syllable bears a tone (or is spoken at a particular pitch); b. again, as in all languages, there are at least two different tones (some K-Y dialects have two tones, High and Low; others have three, Extra-high, High and Low); c. while some dialects prohibit certain tonal combinations, generally any syllable can bear any tone (which is what makes tone lexically distinctive). [p. 195]
new_statements.citation: Ford, Kevin. 1993. A preliminary comparison of Kamano-Yagaria. Language and Linguistics in Melanesia 24(2): 191-202.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lexical tone on every syllable; 2 tones (H/L) in some K-Y dialects, 3 (EH/H/L) in others (EH shown for Move, Kami, Kafe; Yate has c. 95% HL disyllables, p. 200); nothing said about stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Yate lacks EH tone and the stable/unstable distinction (p. 200); Move has stable vs unstable word-final tones with sandhi (pp. 196-197)
